extracted.intended_audience: fiction writers (novelists and short-story authors) working on structuring narrative and worldbuilding
extracted.subtask_description: Advice and evaluative principles for using a 'story within a story' (framing) structure in fiction — when to use it, how to place it, and what effects it should produce. Includes practical artifact-writing homework (letters, journals, almanacs) and pacing/structural considerations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Give mythical or mystical feeling
rubrics_metrics.description: The story-within-a-story structure can give a mythical or mystical feeling to a work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the embedded narrative to create an aura of myth or mystery; the structure creates an element of discovery as readers uncover the link between the frame and the inner story. Examples cited: Cloud Atlas, 10,000 Doors of January, Neverending Story.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adds essential information or explanations
rubrics_metrics.description: An embedded story or artifact can add essential information or explanations needed to understand the present narrative.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the inner story to supply exposition (e.g., explain magic, reveal backstory) without heavy-handed authorial explanation. Example: a found journal that explains present events.

rubrics_metrics.name: Illuminate theme without soapboxing
rubrics_metrics.description: Use the embedded story to illuminate the work's theme more directly without coming off as didactic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Put thematic exploration inside the inner narrative so it feels organic; the frame gives space to explore a lesson or theme subtly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make the work feel richer via smaller narratives
rubrics_metrics.description: Smaller embedded narratives or micro-stories can enrich the main story and give cultural/contextual depth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even if the device is not a major structural element, short legends, interludes, or micro-stories (e.g., Darmok reference, brief cultural tales) provide texture and contrast that deepen reader experience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Useful for twists and reveals
rubrics_metrics.description: Embedding another story is especially useful for twists and reveals because it encourages the reader to solve how the inner story relates to the present narrative.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exploit the reader's curiosity about whether the embedded tale is symbolic, fictional within the world, or another reality; withhold or reveal connections deliberately to create surprise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose frame architecture: single frame vs collage
rubrics_metrics.description: Decide whether the work will have one frame around a single inner story or a 'photo-collage' frame containing many little stories.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A single, large frame can make a work feel epic (e.g., Hyperion/Frankenstein framing), while a collage/mosaic of many embedded stories is good for complex puzzles that resolve across pieces (e.g., Canterbury Tales, One Thousand and One Nights).

rubrics_metrics.name: Frame lends verisimilitude and trust
rubrics_metrics.description: A frame can lend a sense of verisimilitude: a present-day narrator or witness makes the embedded tale feel like a true thing being shared.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use an anchored narrator or 'here-and-now' guide to increase reader trust in the account and to contextualize fantastical or improbable inner narratives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Frames control pacing and provide emotional distance
rubrics_metrics.description: Interludes and frame passages can be used to control pacing and create emotional distance across time jumps.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Placing intermissions or frame interjections between scenes can act as entractes, easing time skips or giving readers breathing room; decide whether the frame is only peripheral or interleaved with the main action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use embedded artifacts as concrete devices
rubrics_metrics.description: Practical devices for the inner story include letters, diary entries, in-world almanacs, spellbooks, and similar artifacts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Homework: take or create an artifact in your WIP and flesh it out into a scene or chapter to see how it adds worldbuilding, plot, or character detail. Artifacts can unlock revelations and new plot directions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use the technique as a writer's scaffold when stuck
rubrics_metrics.description: Writing a smaller embedded story can help an author clarify what they want to say when they are stuck on the larger work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat an inner story as an encapsulated, straightforward version of the idea: explore purpose and meaning in the micro-story, then use that as a guide to build or move the larger narrative forward.

rubrics_metrics.name: Decide whether the embedded tale is 'real' in-universe
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider whether the inner story is diegetically real, a fable, or another reality — ambiguity is a design choice with narrative consequences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Manage reader expectations about the ontology of the embedded tale (is it literally happening in the world, or symbolic?) as part of the technique for mystery, explanation, or thematic resonance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Engage readers to draw their own parallels
rubrics_metrics.description: Withholding explanation for why an embedded story appears engages readers by letting them draw parallels and build personal connections to the material.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Don't over-explain the source or purpose of embedded material; letting readers interpret connections can create an intimate relationship with the work and multiple individualized readings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ensure the frame serves the emotional experience
rubrics_metrics.description: Don't add a frame merely out of habit or writerly insecurity; the frame must serve the emotional experience you want the reader to have.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether the framing device enhances focus, pacing, theme, or verisimilitude; if it doesn't, reconsider using it. Historically frames sometimes existed for practical reasons, but modern writers should choose intentionally.

rubrics_metrics.name: Frames can provide cultural context and history
rubrics_metrics.description: Embedded stories can convey cultural background, legends, or historical figures that inform the main narrative.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use short legends, historical interludes, or fabricated lore to explain references and provide context for characters' actions or societal beliefs (example: Greenbone Saga interludes, Hungarian folk story in The Sun, the Moon, and the Stars).
